title: 1  Exploring Data
text:
1.1 Overview
In these notes we will look at a few common methods for visualizing data. There are two main types of data we will be concerned with in this class: categorical and quantitative data. Categorical data is when the results are descriptive and can be organized into a finite number of answers (or categories). Examples of categorical data include: favorite color, blood type, methods of transportation, favorite food, etc. Quantitative data is data that is numerical and the numbers are representative of actual amounts. This can include: weights, heights, times, exam scores, etc.
The tools we use to visualize data depend on whether the data is categorical or quantatative.

title: 1  Exploring Data
text:
1.4 Histograms
Bar and pie charts are a great way to visualize categorical data. Now we want to address ways to visualize quantitative data, or data that is in the form of numbers.

Example 1.5 (Quantitative Data) Some example of quantitative data include: test scores, age, height, weight, (systolic) blood pressure, etc.

A good way to look at quantitative data is to use a histogram. A histogram breaks the range of all possible values into smaller intervals, then counts how many observation fall into each window. This looks kind of like a bar chart, but the bars sit right next to each other.

Example 1.6 Students in a calculus class obtain the following scores on the midterm exam,
\[100, 85, 91, 76, 88, 82, 95, 62, 84, 79, 90, 73, 87, 81, 92, 77, 86, 83, 80, 89, 74, 93, 85, 79, 82\]
The lowest score is a 62 and the highest score is 100. Let’s break down the range \([60,100]\) into intervals of length 5.



Interval
Count




(60,65]
1


(65,70]

(70,75]
2


(75,80]
5


(80,85]
7


(85,90]

(95,100]

From this we can make a histogram.





A histogram of test scores.





It is typical to call the intervals of a histogram bins, although the reading on WAMAP will call them classes. A histogram should always have bins of the same length. It can be misleading to use different bin lengths in the same way it is misleading to use breaks on the vertical axis of bar charts.






ImportantHistogram Versus Bar Chart



Histogram “bars” touch, while bar chart bars do not. Why do you think this distinction is made?








TipAnswer





Histogram bars touch because the bins cover a continuous range of numbers with no gaps between them. Bar chart bars are separated because each bar is a distinct category, and there’s nothing connecting the categories together.



Most computer programs will set automatic bin sizes based on the distribution of the data you get it, although you will typically have an option to manually input bin specifications. In StatCrunch you are give the optional inputs of the starting value and the bin width.






ImportantBin Endpoints



For whatever computer program you use, make sure you know how the endpoints of your bin intervals are treated. In Example Example 1.6, I wrote intervals like (70,75] which means 70 is excluded from the bin and 75 is included in the bin. The statistical programming language R (what generates the graphs in these notes) uses right inclusive bins, however StatCrunch and Google Sheets use left inclusive bins.


The histograms below represent the same data, just with different bin sizes.








Figure 1.2: Histograms of the same dataset with different bin widths.






Example 1.7 Discuss the following with a partner or two:

Which histogram do you think is better for the above data set and why?
What goes wrong if bins are too wide? What if bins are too narrow?
Is there one “correct” bin width?
Could someone manipulate bin size to mislead the public about a dataset?



Example 1.8 (Histograms on StatCrunch) Reopen the customer dataset in StatCrunch. Create a histogram of customer ages by going to Graph > Histogram.


Example 1.9 (High Tide Heights) The following histogram shows 60 high tide heights over the month of July at a beach. What percentage of high tides were more than 2 meters?








Figure 1.3: Histograms of high tide heights in July.












TipAnswer





We want to compute,
\[\frac{\text{high tides over 2 m}}{\text{total number of high tides}}\cdot 100,\]
where multiply by 100 turns the decimal into a percent. The total number of high tides is 60 as stated in the problem. If not given explicitly, we could carefully sum the quantity in each bin.
The number of high tides that were more than 2 meters is given by the total in the last two bins, \(6+1=7\).
\[ \frac{7}{60}\cdot 100 \approx 11.67\%\]









ImportantInformation Lost



What kinds of information do we lose by only seeing a histogram of the data?


We can use words to descibe the shape of distributions. Some common terms are:

A distribution is symmetric if the left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other.
A distribution is skewed right if it has a long tail stretching to the right. Most values are low, with a few unusually high values.
A distribution is skewed left if it has a long tail stretching to the left. Most values are high, with a few unusually low values.

The direction of the skew is the direction of the tail, not the direction of the peak. A skewed-right distribution has its peak on the left.
We also describe distributions by their number of peaks. A distribution with one peak is unimodal, and a distribution with two clear peaks is bimodal. The symmetric and skewed examples below are all unimodal.








Figure 1.4: Four common distribution shapes.












Shape
Real World Examples




Symmetric
Adult heights (for one sex), repeated measurements of the same quantity, standardized test scores


Skewed right
Household income, home prices, number of social media followers, time spent waiting in line


Skewed left
Scores on an easy exam, age at death in countries with high life expectancy


Bimodal
Customers in a restaurant, shoe sizes of a population not separated by gender









ImportantWhy Bimodal?



A bimodal distribution often means the data contains two different groups mixed together. For the restaurant example, what are the two groups? Can you think of another variable that might be bimodal?



Example 1.10 (Plant Heights) A biology class grew 40 bean plants under identical conditions and measured each plant’s height, in centimeters, after six weeks. The histogram below shows the results.





Histogram of bean plant heights after six weeks.





What is the bin width of this histogram?
Describe the shape of the distribution. Around what height is the center?
What percentage of plants grew taller than 20 cm?
What percentage of plants had heights between 14 and 20 cm?
Can you tell from the histogram how tall the shortest plant is?








TipAnswer






Each bin covers 2 cm, for example 16 to 18 cm.
The distribution is roughly symmetric: the tallest bar is in the middle, at 16–18 cm, and the bars decrease at about the same rate on both sides. The center is around 17 cm.
The last two bins contain plants taller than 20 cm: \(4 + 2 = 6\) plants. \[\frac{6}{40} \cdot 100 = 15\%\]
The bins from 14 to 20 cm contain \(8 + 11 + 9 = 28\) plants. \[\frac{28}{40} \cdot 100 = 70\%\]
No. We only know the shortest plant is somewhere between 10 and 12 cm. The histogram does not show individual values.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.1 Measures of Center
We’ve given a few examples of ways to visualize data, now we want to talk about some important summary statistics. Summary statistics are quantitative values one can use help describe the shape of a distribution. We will talk about measures of center and measures of spread.
Almost always, summary statistics can only be used on quantitative data.
The goal of measures of center is to describe the value of a typical datapoint. There are three measures of center we will cover:
\[\bar{x} = \frac{x_1+x_2+ \cdots + x_n}{n}.\]
The difference between the median and mean of a distribution can reveal information about the shape of the distribution. In particular, if a distribution is skewed or symmetric.
Figure 2.1: Right-skewed household income distribution.
When a distribution is skewed, the mean is pulled more towards the tail than the median.
Figure 2.2: Approximately symmetric distribution of soccer team heights.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
Mode: The value(s) with the highest frequency in the dataset. Mode is the only measure of center that can be used with categorical data.
Mean: The average of the values. If a dataset has \(n\) values \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(\dots\), \(x_n\), then the mean \(\bar{x}\) is given by



Median: The midpoint of the distribution. It is the number such that half the observations fall above and half fall below.


Example 2.1 (Classroom Ages) A college class has 22 students with the following ages: 18, 22, 21, 21, 21, 18, 20, 42, 23, 44, 18, 18, 21, 18, 22, 18, 22, 23, 20, 38, 20, 34. Compute the mean, median, and mode.
See this data on StatCrunch to perform the computations there.







TipAnswer





To compute the mode and median it helps to order the data from smallest to largest.
\[18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 20, 20, 20, 21, 21, 21, 21, 22, 22, 22, 23, 23, 34, 38, 42, 44\]
The mode is 18, which occurs in the dataset 6 times.
Since the dataset is 22 students, the median is the value in-between the 11th and 12th observations. The 11th and 12th observation both happen to be 21, therefore the median is 21.
The mean is,
\[\frac{6 \cdot 18 + 3 \cdot 20 + 4 \cdot 21 + 3 \cdot 22 + 2 \cdot 23  + 34 + 42 + 44}{22} = \frac{522}{22} = 23.73.\]
Notice that the mean is slightly larger than the median this is because there are a handful of older students with outlier ages. The mean gets pulled by outliers more than the median does.









ImportantMedian on Datasets of Even Size



For this course, to compute the median when the dataset has an even number of observations average the two observation in the middle. This is a typical convention chosen in statistics.












ImportantMean Versus Median



The reason outliers pull the mean more than the median is because mean minimizes the error squared, while the median minimizes the absolute error. Squaring the error means outliers will have extra impact. This fact is outside of the scope of this course, but I am happy to chat about it for curious minds!



Example 2.2 (Creating Data) Using StatCrunch complete the following:

Create a dataset of 10 student ages where the median is 20 and at least one student is not 20.
Is it possible to do this and have no student be 20 years old?
If we increased the size of the dataset to 15 students can you still create a dataset with median 20 and no students are 20 years old?








TipAnswer






One possible answer: 18, 18, 18, 19, 20, 20, 20, 21, 22, 23.
Yes it is! Since the dataset has an even size, we can make it so the 5th entry is 19 and the 6th entry is 21. Such as: 18, 18, 18, 19, 19, 21, 22, 23, 25.
This is not possible if the dataset has an odd size. When there are 15 students, the age of the 8th youngest student is the median–so that student must be 20.





Example 2.3  

Using StatCrunch or Google Sheets, create a dataset of 25 non-negative integers (e.g. whole numbers 0 and larger) where the mean is less than the median. Plot the histogram of the data.
(Challenge) If I have a dataset of 25 non-negative integers and the median is 50, what is the smallest possible mean?








TipAnswer






Your dataset should be skewed to the left in this example.
The smallest possible mean occurs when 12 data points have value 0 and 13 have the value 50. This guarantees the median is 50. So the mean is

\[\frac{12 \cdot 0 + 13 \cdot 50}{25} = 26.\]
We can’t make any of numbers smaller or else we would either change the median or break the non-negative rule. Making any of the numbers bigger would increase the mean!









ImportantWhen to use mode?



Discuss: what might be a situation where the mode is the most relevant summary statistic to use?








Tip





Mode is the only measure of center that can be used for categorical data. Also, mode is great for bimodal (or multimodal) distributions!









ImportantNobody’s Average



In 1950 the airforce measured 140 physical dimension of 4063 pilots and designed the cockpit to match he average (mean) dimensions. Lieutenant Gilbert S. Daniels then compared this “average pilot” to individual pilot records to show that no pilot was within 15% of the average on the ten most relevant dimensions. In other words, the cockpits were designed to fit no one! Thus lead to the adaptation of adjustable seats.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.2 Measures of Spread

Example 2.4 (Commute Times) Data on StatCrunch. The below histograms depict the commute time of 500 people who work in Town A and Town B. How are the datasets similar and how are they different?








Figure 2.3: Commute times in two different towns.






The above example illustrates that it is important to have statistics that describe the spread of a distribution. There are a few we will investigate today.

2.2.1 Range
The range of a dataset is the largest observation minus the smallest observation.

Example 2.5 The commute times data is given here. Compute the range of the commuting data for each town.







TipAnswer





For Town A, the longest and shortest commute times are 42 and 18 minutes, respectively. So the range for Town A is \(42-18 = 24\).
For Town B, the longest and shortest commute times are 62 and 1 minute, respectively. So the range for Town B is \(62-1 = 61\).



Range does give us an initial look at the spread of the distribution, but outliers can obfuscate how range relates to spread. Consider two classes with the following histograms of exam scores:








Figure 2.4: Scores on Exam 1 in Class A and Class B





The range of both distributions is (approximately) the same, but the spread looks very different. Only 2 out of 20 students scored below a 60 in Class A, while 8 students (out of 20) scored below a 60 in Class B.


2.2.2 Inter-Quartile Range (IQR)
Recall that the median divides the observations into two parts of equal size. This is because we defined the median as the value which half the observations are below and half are above. Quartiles divide the data into 4 equal parts. Specifically we define:

The first quartile (or lower quartile), Q1, is the value such that 25% of the data lies below this value.
The second quartile (or median), M, is value where 50% of the data lies below this value.
The third quartile (or upper quartile), Q3, is the value such that 75% of the data lies below this value.

Computing the min, Q1, Q2, Q3, and max of a data set is known as the five-number summary.






Important



Note that Q1 and Q3 are computed differently on Google Sheets than on StatCrunch (and in this class). While they are effectively the same, it will sometimes cause incorrect homework answers.

ImportantIQR Versus Range



Why might IQR be seen as a better gauge of spread than range?




2.2.3 Outliers
An outlier is an oberservation that lies far away from the general distribution. The readings define outliers as points that are:

Smaller than \(\text{Q}1 - 1.5 \cdot (\text{IQR})\), or
Larger than \(\text{Q}3 + 1.5 \cdot (\text{IQR})\).

Do not think of this as a set in stone rule. In fact, the multiplier 1.5 was not chosen with any real mathematical theory behind it. Use these values to flag potential outliers in the dataset, but context is an important factor when determining what is an outlier. Moreover, do not automatically remove outliers from a dataset

\[\text{lower} = 29.5 - 1.5(10) = 14.5, \quad \text{upper} = 39.5 + 15 = 54.5\]

There is a false notion that outliers should be removed from the data set but this is not true! Outliers should be expected in data and are part of the underlying distribution.
Only remove data points if they are the result of mistake in data entry or collection, or if they can be explained by a fundamentally different process which you are not interested in investigating.

2.3 Boxplots
Boxplots are a way to visualize the five number summary as well as outliers. Let’s see this with an example.

Example 2.9 (Boxplots in StatCrunch) For this example use this data on StatCrunch. To make a boxplot of the data select Graph > Boxplot. Just select annual_income and then compute.

The box of the boxplot goes from Q1 to Q3 and the median is shown as a horizontal line. The two sticks (called whiskers) on either side of the box go until the largest data point that isn’t an outlier and the stars (called fences) indicate outlier values. If we deselect the box indicating “Use fences to identify outliers” in StatCrunch then the whiskers will go all the way until the end of the range.



Labeled boxplot.



Example 2.10 The boxplots below show the typed words per minutes for support agents and software engineers. Compare the two distributions using what you know about boxplots.



Typing speed boxplots for support agents and software engineers.









TipAnswer





The median support agent is a faster typer than the median software engineer. Software engineers have a much larger variation in typing speeds then support agents.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.4 Standard Deviation
Here we will define and use the sample standard deviation. This is slightly different, but related to, the population standard deviation as well as the variance. These are terms we will define explicitly later. Given data points \(x_1\), , \(x_n\) the sample standard deviation is defined by the formula
\[SD = \sqrt{\frac{(x_1-\bar{x})^2 + (x_2-\bar{x})^2 + \cdots + (x_n - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]
where \(\bar{x}\) denotes the mean of the dataset. Let’s see this formula in action with a small example,

Example 2.11 Anna denotes how many Reese’s Peanutbutter Cups her 10 friends eat at a party. She gets the following amounts:
\[3, 4, 3, 6, 6, 2, 1, 8, 5, 5.\]
Compute the mean and standard deviation of the dataset.







TipAnswer





Let’s compute the mean,
\[\bar{x} = \frac{3+4+3+6+6+2+1+8+5+5}{10} = \frac{43}{10} = 4.3.\]
Next compute the differences,
\[-1.3,-0.3,-1.3,1.7,1.7,-2.3,-3.3,3.7,0.7,0.7.\]
Square and sum,
\[ 1.69 + 0.09 + 1.69 + 2.89 + 2.89 + 5.29 + 10.89 + 13.69 + 0.49 + 0.49 = 40.1 \]
Now divide by \(n-1 = 10-1 = 9\) and take the square root,
\[SD = \sqrt{\frac{40.1}{9}} = \sqrt{4.456} \approx 2.11.\]



We claim that standard deviation is telling us something about the spread of the distribution, but we can be more precise than that. The standard deviation tell us the average distance from an given datapoint to the mean. A larger standard deviation means the data is more spread out, while a smaller standard deviation tells us the data is compact.

title: 2  Summary Statistics
text:
2.5 Normal Distribution and the 68-95-99.7
Quantitative data is normally distributed when its distribution looks like a symmetric “mound” or “bell” shape.





Histogram of approximately normal data.




Things that are approximately normal in distribution include:

Baby birth weights
Heights of adults by sex
Blood pressure of adults
Standardized testing scores

Statistics over time may have you thinking everything is normal, but this is not true! You should always question whether a distribution is normal or has some other distribution. Things that are not normal include:

Income
Time between earthquakes in a given region
Number of shots taken in a soccer game
Amount of time someone waits in a line

If a distribution is normal though, the empirical rule (or 68-95-99.7 rule) gives us a rough estimate of what percentage of the data falls withing 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean. We have:

68% of the data falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean
95% of the data falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean
99.7% falls within 3 standard deviations of the mean











Example 2.14 (Baby Weights) The mean birth weight at a hospital is 7.3 lbs with a standard deviation of 1.1 lbs. Assume that the birth weight is approximately normally distributed.

What percentage of babies weigh between 6.2 lbs and 8.4 lbs?
What percentage of babies weigh less than 4.0 lbs?

title: 3  Examining Relationships
text:
3.1 Side-by-Side Boxplots (C \(\to\) Q)
In Topic 1 we looked at ways to visualize data about a single variable. Now we want to learn ways to examine the relationship between two variables.
When we look at two variable we are interested in how one impacts the other. The response variable or dependent variable is the variable that gives the outcome of the study. The explanatory variable is the variable that claims to impact the response variable.
If the explanatory variable is categorical and the response variable is quantitative, then one way to visualize the potential differences in distribution is by using side-by-side boxplots.
Another method of visualizing relationships between a categorical explanatory variable and a quantitative response variable is by using a stacked histogram.
Figure 3.2: Stacked histogram of goals scored by different positions.
Here we see that the histogram is colored by player position. From this visualization we can see that defenders typically don’t score much.
StatCrunch will let you do something similar, although it won’t let you exactly stack the bars like above. In StatCrunch you can choose Graph > Histogram. Then you can select your response variable and group by your explanatory variable. Scroll all the way down to the multiple graph section and select the same X and Y axis. You can also use the rows and columns per page to change how many histograms are viewed at once.

title: 3  Examining Relationships
text:
Example 3.2 Below is a dataset of 189 births from a 1986 study at Baystate Medical Center (in Massachusetts). What similarities and differences do you notice between babies born from smokers versus nonsmokers? What can you not tell by the boxplots that you might be interested in knowing about the data?








Figure 3.1: Side-by-side boxplots of birth weight based on mother’s smoking status.












TipAnswer





From the bokplot it looks like the average baby weight is higher for nonsmoking mothers, however there is a large overlap in the IQR. The lower end of the boxplots look similar.
I would be interesting in learning how many participants were smokers/nonsmokers, which we cannot tell from the boxplots.









ImportantAssociation does not equal causation!



There may be a lurking variable which affects both the explanatory and response variable. This is why you should be careful about drawing conclusions just from statistical data.
Good study design should help eliminate potential lurking variables, however they are impossible to completely eliminate.



Example 3.3 What are potential lurking variables that could impact the study in Example Example 3.2?

3.3 Scatterplots (Q -> Q)

Example 3.7 We want to determine if more time spent studying improves the score received on an exam. The amount of time spent studying was self reported by students. Open the data in StatCrunch.
Since we want to know if study time improves exam score, the explanatory variable is study time and the response variable is exam score. We can plot these using a scatter plot (Graph > Scatter Plot). We should set the study time as the x variable and the exam score as the y variable.









Figure 3.3: Scatter plot of time spent studying and exam scores.





We see from the scatter plot that hours spent studying is positively correlated with exam scores. This means that the more hours spent studying, the higher of an exam score a student tends to receive. Notice that the points appear to show a “fuzzy” line with a positive slope.
Average hours of exercise weekly is negatively correlated with resting heart rate. This means the more hours exercised, the lower the resting heart rate.

We use the words strong, moderate and weak to describe how linearly correlated the data is. Below is an example of each,








Figure 3.5: Strength of correlation.





Above the value \(r\) is the correlation coefficient for the data. Don’t worry about the formula for computing r as we will use StatCrunch for this computation. See how to use it below,

Example 3.8 (Correlation Coefficient) Open this data in StatCrunch. Make a scatter plot with longevity as the explanatory variable and gestation period as the response variable. Then compute the correlation coefficient of the data.

The correlation coefficient \(r\) can measure the strength of the correlation, but only after we use the scatterplot to justify that it is linear! If our data is approximately linear, then the sign of the correlation coefficient tells us whether it is positive or negatively correlated. The magnitude of the correlation coefficient tells us the strength. There are a lot of different bench marks you will see for what \(r\) value is “moderate” versus “strong.” You should think of these benchmarks as a guideline and that they are context dependent.
Plenty of data is not linearly correlated! Let’s see some examples.








Figure 3.6: Daily home energy use is highest on cold and hot days and lowest at mild temperatures.

title: 3  Examining Relationships
text:
3.4 Linear Regression
If we do feel a line is linear we can perform least-squares linear regression. This creates a line that best fits the data. We will not do this by hand, we will use StatCrunch. It is important to be able to interpret the StatCrunch output though.

Example 3.9 Open this data in StatCrunch. Perform the linear regression on the data. What is the equation for the line of best fit? Write a sentence to interpret the slope in the context of the explanatory and response variables.








Figure 3.8: Longevity and gestation period for a variety of animals.












TipAnswer





Under the table Parameter Estimates we want to look at the intercept and slope estimate values to generate the line of best fit.
Intercept: 21.71
Slope: 13.13
Recall that longevity is our response variable–this means for our line it is the input (x variable). Gestation will be the output (y variable). So our line has the form,
\[\text{gestation} = 13.13\times(\text{longevity}) + 21.71\]
The slope tells us that, on average, each year of longevity amounts to an additional 13.13 days of gestation. The intercept tells us for a animal with a longevity of 0 years, the gestation period is, on average, 21.71 days. This is an impossible scenario though, so it is outside of our domain of interest.




Example 3.10 Use the line of best fit computed in Example Example 3.9 to approximate the gestation period of a North American river otter, which has a typical lifespan of 12 years.







TipAnswer





Using our line, we estimate that the North American river otter will have a gestation period of \(13.13\times 12 + 21.71 = 179.27\) months.
According the the internet, the river otters have a gestation period of 285-375 days due to a process called delayed implantation. The more you know, eh?!









ImportantEstimation



You should avoid using linear regression to estimate values that fall outside of the range of your data. When we zoom in on functions they almost always look linear, but zooming out can reveal more complicated behavior. Just because a line fits the data you have, doesn’t mean it will still look linear when we “zoom out.”
For example, the line in Example Example 3.9 should not be used to approximate the gestation time of an ORca, which averages 90 years of life. Plugging this in gives an approximate gestation period of 1,203 days or ~40 months–much longer than their actual gestation period of 15-18 months.

title: 4  Sampling and Study Design
text:
4.1 Sampling
Sampling is the way we select participants for a study. Sampling design is crucial for creating an unbiased study.
Simple random sampling involves selecting randomly from the entire population. In practice, there are many limiting factors involved in generating a truly simple random sample.
We refer to the sampling frame as the actual population where the sample was taken from. Like in the above example, the sampling frame can be different from the intended population.
Systematic sampling is when we choose from the population in a systematic fashion, e.g. picking every 5th name in an alphabetized list, picking every 3rd person to show up at a clinic.
Cluster sampling is when we break the population down into clusters, randomly select some of the clusters, and use every individual in the selected clusters.
Stratified sampling is when we break down a population into strata and sample randomly from each strata. This is a good type of sampling to do if you can identify potential groupings in the population where you expect major differences.
Multistage sampling is when a mix of methods is applied to different levels.

title: 4  Sampling and Study Design
text:
Example 4.1 (Simple Random Sample) What is the intended population of each study? How do the following random samples fail to reflect the entire population or be genuinely random?

A city wants to know how adult residents feel about expanding bus service. Planners get the list of every account on the city’s water and electric billing system and randomly select 1,000 accounts to survey.
A polling firm wants to estimate support for a ballot measure among adults in Ohio. It buys a list of all published residential phone numbers in the state and uses software to randomly select 1,500 numbers to call.
A grocery store chain wants to know how satisfied its customers are with checkout wait times. It pulls the list of all transactions from the past month in its system and randomly selects 500 of them. It then contacts each matched customer through the email linked to their loyalty account.








TipAnswer






They are only sampling from names listed on a utility bill. Those who live with roommate ro cooperative housing are excluded from the survey.
This survey is excluding households without a landline, which could lead to bias in the sample.
There are two main issues with this. The survey is not truly random because customers who shop more are more likely to get contacted. Additionally, only those signed up for rewards are contacted.










Cluster Sampling. Image generated by Claude.



Example 4.2 When it is a bad idea to use cluster sampling?







TipAnswer





Don’t use cluster sampling if your clusters vary widely in make up (with relation to your survey). For example, suppose I was asking the question “Does your household have access to a car?” Clustering by cities in the Sound are would be a bad idea, as we expect those in Seattle & Tacoma to have lower rates of car access than a Bainbridge Island or Gig Harbor.







Stratified Sampling. Image Generated by Claude.



Example 4.3 (Stratified Sampling) The county transit authority wants to estimate the percentage of Cuyahoga County (Cleveland, OH and surrounding area) households that don’t have access to a car, to help plan bus routes. They decided to use stratified sampling to pick a random sample of the county population. For each city/town in the county they sample roughly 15% of the population.







ImportantClusters Versus Strata



There’s no difference in the meaning between the terms cluster and strata. In both cases we are breaking the population down into groups.






An example of multistage sampling. Image generated with Claude.



Example 4.4 (Identify the Sampling) For each scenario identify the type of sampling used as simple, systematic, cluster, or stratified.

A teacher of a 500 person lecture wants to know how much time students on average on each homework assignment. The class contains freshmen, sophomores, and juniors, so the teach randomly selects 50 students from each class to sample.
A grocery store manager wants to estimate customer satisfaction. Starting with a randomly chosen customer among the first 20 to check out on Saturday, the manager surveys every 20th customer who passes through the checkout line for the rest of the day.
A school district wants to know how many hours per week high school students spend on extracurricular activities. The district has 40 homerooms, so it randomly selects 6 homerooms and surveys every student in those homerooms.








TipAnswer






This is stratified sampling, since we choose a random sample from each class.
This is systematic sampling.
This is cluster sampling, since we survey all the student in each homeroom.

title: 4  Sampling and Study Design
text:
4.2 Study Design
There are three types of study design we will focus on learning:

An observational study is when participants are asked about their variables in their life without researcher interference. An observational study is prospective if variables are recorded as they happen. An observational study is retrospective if participants recall information about the past.
A survey is where where participants are asked to report on certain variables related to themselves, typically through a form, survey, or interview.
An experiment is when researchers interfere instead of measuring variables as they occur naturally. Researchers assign the explanatory variable to participants and see how it impacts the response variables.







ImportantSurveys



A survey is a type observational study, however it earns a distinction because surveys ask participants to express their feelings/opinions. An observational study (not survey), typically relies on observation, tracking, or medical records.



Example 4.5 (Study Types) Determine whether each study is an observational study, survey, or experiment.

Students are randomly assigned to study with or without music, then take the same quiz.
A school emails parents a questionnaire asking how satisfied they are with the lunch menu.
Doctors review hospital records to compare heart disease rates in smokers and non-smokers.
Tomato plants are randomly given one of three fertilizers, and their yields are measured.
A pollster calls 1,000 voters and asks which candidate they plan to support.

observational study (prospective)
experiment
survey
observational study (retrospective)
experiment
survey

title: 4  Sampling and Study Design
text:
4.3 Causation and Experiments
A good experiment should use randomization to control for other factors potentially impacting the response variable.
Consider an experiment where we trying to measure the efficacy of a new weight loss drug. The explanatory variable in this case is the new drug and the response variable would be measures of weight loss.
In the experiment split individuals into atreatment group, who receive the drug and a control group who receive do not receive the drug. These groups should be randomly assigned and we should do so in a way that makes the two groups similar with respect to other factors that could impact weight loss.

Example 4.6 What are other factors we might want to control for when randomly assigning our groups?

Another good idea would be to make the experiment blind this means the participants should not know whether they are in the treatment or control group as it could impact their behavior. We could administer a placebo to the control group.
We could go even further and make the experiment double-blind meaning that even the researchers don’t know what group the participant was assigned to.

Example 4.7 Give an example of an experiment that is impossible to make blind. Give an example of an experiment that could be blind, but not double-blind.

title: 4  Sampling and Study Design
text:
4.4 Survey Questions
Survey questions should be carefully thought through in order to be effective. When drafting questions, one should:

Think about whether a question is better open or closed,
Avoid planting ideas or leading questions,
Avoid complicated questions addressing more than one idea,
Avoid unbalanced response options.

title: 5  Basics of Probability
text:
5.1 Random Experiments, Sample Space, and Outcomes
The probability of an event is the likelihood of the event occurring. If we denote an event by \(E\) then we write
\[P(E)\]
to denote the probability that event \(E\) happens. Probabilities should be numbers between 0 and 1.
\[E \text{ is impossible} \implies P(E) = 0.\] \[E \text{ always occurs} \implies P(E) = 1.\]
An event has a theoretical probability, where we infer the probability from the nature of the situation.
We can also use data to conjecture probabilities. We will call this an empirical probability.
According to the Law of Large Numbers the empirical probability should be close to the theoretical probability if the number of random experiments is large.
The coin flip example is silly because the theoretical probability is easily attainable. Empirical probability are useful when the actually theoretical probabilities are not attainable.
A random experiment is a process that can be repeated under the same conditions, where all possible outcomes are known in advance but the outcome of any single trial cannot be predicted. Examples include,
An outcome is any possible result of the experiment. The sample space of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes.
Notice that \(TH\) and \(HT\) are two different outcome–order matters in this experiment.
With our definition of sample space, we can redefine an event as a subset of the sample space.

title: 5  Basics of Probability
text:
5.2 Naive Probability
If all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely, then the problem of an event is
\[P(E) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in the event}}{\text{size of the sample space}}.\]

Example 5.11 What is the probability of flipping a coin three times and getting exactly 1 head?







TipAnswer





From earlier we know the sample space has 8 events. All of these events are equally likely. The outcomes with exactly one head are:: HTT, THT, TTH. So the probability is \(3/8 = 0.375\).




Example 5.12 A coin is flip 3 times or until a head is flipped. What is the sample space? Can I use the naive probability definition to compute the probability of flipping at least 1 tail? Explain.







Tip





The sample space is,
\[\{H, TH, TTH \}.\]
I cannot use the naive definition because the three outcomes are not equally likely.




Example 5.13 Two 6-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is less than 6?







TipAnswer





The sample space is the same as in the solution to Example Example 5.10. All of these events are equally likely, so we can compute the probability by denoting how many outcomes have sum less than 6:
\[11, \, 12, \, 13, \, 14, \, 21, \, 22, \, 23, \, 31, \, 32, \, 41.\]
So the probability is \(10/36 = 0.278\).

title: 5  Basics of Probability
text:
5.3 Rules of Probability
The complement of an event \(A\) is all outcomes where \(A\) does not happen.

Example 5.14 (Complement) Suppose I roll a 6-sided dice. Let \(A\) be the event that I roll a number divisible by 3. Therefore
\[P(A) = \frac{2}{6} \approx 0.33.\]
The complement of \(A\), denoted \(A^c\) is the event that I roll a number not divisible by three, e.g. 1, 2, 4, or 5. Thus,
\[P(A^c) = \frac{4}{6} \approx 0.67.\]

For an event and its complement, the following relationship holds
\[\boxed{P(A) = 1 - P(A^c)}\]

Example 5.15 State the complement of the following events. You do not need to compute any probabilities.

The event that a randomly selected patient has blood type O.
I roll two 6-sided dice. Let \(A\) be the event that the sum of the roll is at least 10.
A flip a coin until I flip heads. Let \(A\) be the event that I get heads by the 10th flip.
I roll two 6-sided dice. Let \(A\) be the event that neither roll is a 6.


In some instances, it is easier to compute the probability of the complement. Thus we can use the boxed relationship to speed up the problem.

Example 5.16 I roll two 6-sided dice. Compute the probability that the sum of the two dice is at least 3.







TipAnswer





We know that there are 36 outcomes when rolling a dice twice. Three of those outcomes sum to less than 3: 11, 12, 21. So the probability of rolling at least a 3 is,
\[1 - \frac{3}{36}  = \frac{33}{36} \approx 0.92.\]



Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The union of \(A\) and \(B\), \(A \cup B\), is the event where at least one of the happens. For example, suppose I randomly select a person on the street and let
\[A = \text{the person has a dog}, \; B = \text{the person has a cat}.\]
Then the union is
\[A \cup B = \text{the person has a dog \textbf{or} a cat}.\]
The intersection of \(A\) and \(B\), \(A \cap B\), is the event where they both happen. So in the example above,
\[A \cup B = \text{the person has a dog \textbf{and} a cat}.\]
Two events are disjoint if it is impossible to satisfy both at the same time. Mathematically, they are disjoint if \(A \cap B\) is impossible (e.g. contains no outcomes).

Example 5.17 Determine whether or not the following events are disjoint.

Roll a dice. \(A\) = the dice shows an even number, \(B\) = the dice shows an odd number.
Roll a dice. \(A\) = the dice shows an even number, \(B\) = the dice shows a number greater than 3.
Flip a coin twice. \(A\) = both flips are heads, \(B\) = at least one flip is tails.
Roll two dice. \(A\) = the sum is 8, \(B\) = both dice show the same number.
Randomly select a high school student. \(A\) = the student is a freshman, \(B\) = the student is a senior.
Randomly select a high school student. \(A\) = the student plays a sport, \(B\) = the student is in band.








TipAnswer






Disjoint, a number cannot be both even and odd.
Not disjoint, for example a roll of 4 satisfies both.
Disjoint.
Not disjoint.
Disjoint.
Not disjoint.




If events \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, we can add their probabilities to compute the probability of the union
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\]
But if two events are not disjoint, we should use the principle of inclusion-exclusion
\[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\]

Example 5.18 A high school has 400 students. Of these, 180 play a sport, 90 are in band, and 40 do both. A student is selected at random.

What is the probability the student plays a sport?
What is the probability that a student is in the band?
What is the probability that a student plays a sport and is in the band?
What is the probability that a student is in the band or plays a sport?
What is the probability a student does neither?








TipAnswer






\(180/400=0.45\).
\(90/400=0.225\)
\(40/400 = 0.1\)
Let \(S\) = plays a sport and \(B\) = in the band. Use inclusion-exclusion,

\[P(S \cup B) = 0.45 + 0.225 - 0.1 = 0.165.\]

Doing neither is the complement of being in band or playing a sport,

\[P((S \cup B)^c) = 1 - P(S \cup B) = 1 - 0.165 = 0.835.\]



Two events are independent if one event happening does not change the probability of the other event happening.

Example 5.19 Consider the events:

It rains today.
It is cloudy today.

These events are not independent, because if we know it is cloudy this increases the chance that it is going to rain. We say these events are dependent.


Example 5.20 Consider the events:

A couples first baby is a girl.
A couples second baby is a girl.

These events are independent, because the sex of the first child has no impact on the sex of the second child.


Example 5.21 Determine whether the following events are independent:

A coin is flipped twice. \(A\): the first flip is heads. \(B\): the second flip is heads.
A coin is flipped twice. \(A\): the first flip is heads. \(B\): at least one flip is heads.
A dice is rolled twice. \(A\): the first roll is even. \(B\): the sum of the two rolls is 7.
A dice is rolled twice. \(A\): the first roll is a 6. \(B\): the sum of the two rolls is at least 10.
\(A\): a patient has blood type O. \(B\): their child has blood type O.
\(A\): the Seattle Mariners win. \(B\): the average on the exam is more than 70%.

For a discrete random variable, whether or not the inequality is strict makes a difference.

Example 6.9 Roll two dice and let \(X\) denote the sum of the rolls. What is \(P(X > 10)\)? What is \(P(X \geq 10)\)?







TipAnswer





The sample space is 36 outcomes that are all equally likely. There is 1 outcome that sums to 12 (66), 2 outcomes that sum to 11 (56, 65), and 3 outcomes that sum to 10 (46, 55, 64). So,
\[P(X > 10) = \frac{3}{36} = \frac{1}{12}\]
and
\[P(X \geq 10) = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}.\]









ImportantInequalities and Cont. RVs



For continuous random variables whether or not the inequality is strict does not change the probability! If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, then
\[P(X > 5) = P(X \geq 5).\]
